result: Goal set: read delivered documents in order, answer detailed questions about the retellings only. This anchors every prompt going forward.

Vira Toland (Ostrey Hollow, 1979): A milk-hauler's daughter recalls the 1919 scandal when milk tester Ansel Keddie was caught stealing cream, ruining families' livelihoods and fracturing lifelong relationships.
The document is the 1966 annual report and does not contain information about road levies recommended for 1908.

Effie Loomis (Association secretary, 1901–1940, writing 1941): A detailed institutional account of the Association's founding and the 1925 arbitration that awarded Ostrey Hollow patrons $3,800 despite finding no wrongdoing.
The play being performed at the Ellerby Playhouse is *The Sparrow Hotel*.

Ansel Keddie (tester, 1925): His defense of thirty years of meticulous testing records and the unsent explanation of the unexplained higher readings and the 1911 measurement incident that caused his family's estrangement.
The total amount of the wholesale order Norcross placed with Purcell & Weare on 14 March 1932 was $59.65.

Ivy Keddie (granddaughter, 1959): Scientific proof that the station's condemned glassware measured 5% short, explaining the entire 26-year testing anomaly and revealing the patrons' true loss of $19,000 versus the $3,800 arbitration award.
Tamsin Ochoa's service number is 4471-K.

Wilbur Teague (bookkeeper, 1905–1945, writing 1948): His explanation of the "station gain" ledger entry—the consistent 5.25% surplus of butterfat received versus credited—and his acknowledgment that he raised concerns once to manager Selby Vose in 1916 but was told to let it alone.
Judge Thurlow Vane imposed a fine of $5.00 on Delia Fought for the petty theft of dress goods.

Merle Strawn (state dairy inspector, 1907–1936, writing 1936): Extracts from his circuit books documenting the June 1923 discovery that Ostrey Hollow's pipettes would not deliver their mark, leading to their condemnation and replacement—the scientific evidence that explains the 26-year testing anomaly.
Lemma 2.1 is named "Interleaving."

Halbert Nym (curator, 1972): Cataloguing the archival evidence of the Ostrey Hollow case—invoices, ledgers, test books, the condemned crate, arbitration minutes, state inspector reports, and Ivy Keddie's 1958 measurements—creating the institutional record.
Mr. Ansgar Krell remained 4 weeks at the Cold Spring Water-Cure for his rheumatism.

Selby Vose (manager, 1926): His defense of the $3,800 award as a peace gesture but assertion that water was deliberately added to Ostrey Hollow cans—evidenced by the sudden 1924 test improvement when scrutiny began—and vindication of his 1919 warning circular.
The error code `SKF-2201` is returned when a sailings query span exceeds 14 days.
Roy Brant, farmer, describing his father's ledger documenting milk delivery weights that inexplicably never disputed the station's despite known testing troubles at Ostrey Hollow.
Dr. Pemberton charged $8.00 for the confinement and mileage for Mrs. Content Averill on January 3, 1906.
Rosalie Cudd, cheesemaker at Alder Corners, testifying that the four Hessel Bottom farmers' milk tested consistently around 3.80 over sixteen summers and was always good quality.
The man's crown will cost him $1,480 after insurance.
Leland Vaught, dairy professor, explaining that defective pipettes at Ostrey Hollow delivered short charges systematically, causing proportionally low butterfat tests for twenty-five years.
The color vermilion is named in the third paragraph, describing the apron worn by Bettine Rausch.

Dell Rundle, schoolteacher, chronicling fifty years of the Larrow Valley Creamery and the unresolved trouble at Ostrey Hollow station where milk tested lower despite the arbitration board finding no cause.
Message No. 219 filed by Perley Dunmore reading "FATHER VERY LOW COME AT ONCE" was 6 words.
Alonzo Frick, arbitration board chairman, recalling the 1925 Ostrey Hollow case where he awarded damages without establishing a cause, and reflecting that the answer eluded them all.
The locksmith's dog is named Buckley, a bad-tempered gray terrier.
Hobart Sill, buttermaker of forty-one years, testifying that Ostrey Hollow cream consistently arrived heavier than weighed, and that he believed water was being added to cans before testing.
The norm defined in Definition 1.3 is called the Trebbin norm.
Nyle Grigg, 1908 committee chairman, defending the finding that wet hay thins cream and citing State Agricultural College Bulletin No. 214 as vindication.

Dr. Roland Kepp, veterinary surgeon, explaining that wet meadow soil causes mineral-deficient herbage that reduces butterfat production, citing College Bulletin No. 214 and dismissing the 1911 interval.
Phyl warns Armando not to use dryer eleven, which takes coins and stops after forty seconds.

Hazel Brant, farmer's daughter and keeper of the weigh book (1981 tape), revealing that the condemned glassware sat unexamined in the loft for twenty years before her cousin Ivy discovered and measured it.
The woman called Tuesday wore a magenta scarf in all weathers.

Duncan Keddie, schoolteacher and Ansel's son (1968 family notes), meticulously mapping family connections and tracing the archive trail of evidence—especially the condemned glass hidden in the loft above the 1925 arbitration.

The jury returned a verdict that Obadiah Chalmers came to his death by accidental drowning in the mill pond, resulting from an accidental fall from the flume edge while at his work, without evidence of any other person's involvement.

*The Ashlin Chronicle* (1958 newspaper), reporting the publication of Bulletin 471 that clears the long-dead Ansel Keddie by proving defective glassware in the condemned crate caused the testing error.
In the spring of 1996, the ice-out pot was six thousand eight hundred and forty dollars.

Junia Ammon, historian of Ammon & Sons glassblowing firm (1949), reproducing the 1897 invoice and the telling 1923 letter that reveals the company knew the pipettes were defective but claimed their records wouldn't tell them anything about the original lot.
In Proposition 4.1, the sharpness example uses a 7-cycle with a pendant path of length two attached to each vertex.

Cleve Oram, cream hauler's son (1977 recording), witnessed the condemned crate in the loft for thirty-five years and recalls his father suspected stolen cream, but Ivy Keddie's discovery proved it was the defective glass.
The start delimiter byte of a BSWP frame is 0xB5.

Orin Falke, county agricultural agent (1959 report), providing a comprehensive chronological summary that refutes the three competing theories and confirms the defective glassware, with an added note withdrawing the wet-hay explanation.
Russ's wife's name is Dorrit.

Bertram Kyle, retired clerk (1953 memoir), revealing that everything was recorded in plain sight—the inspectors' condemnation of the glass, the recurring "station gain" entries—yet nobody laid the documents side by side to look.
The color named in the third paragraph is teal, referring to the endpapers of the collected edition containing the famous diagram.

Orra Keddie, diary extracts (1897-1930, published 1964), chronicling the weight of suspicion on Ansel from the 1902 complaints through the 1925 dismissal, the break with her brother Emmet, and Ansel's final observation that a man cannot be cleared of what nobody will name.
The total toll collected at Wren's Bend bridge for the week of June 5–11, 1899 was $13.88.
